newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour party seeks tighter advertising rules.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour party seeks tighter advertising rules.

text.p: Britain's Labour Party plans to tighten the regulation of advertising if it wins the next election, including imposing fines on advertisers that breach the industry's code of practice, according to a report on Thursday.

The trade publication Campaign said Nigel Griffiths, Labour's shadow consumer affairs minister who is reviewing the party's policy on advertising, disclosed the plans to beef up the Advertising Standards Authority and impose fines on so-called "bad" advertisers.

Britain's advertising industry is self-regulating, with the industry's Advertising Standard Authority setting the code of practice and overseeing compliance. The ASA, which oversees non-broadcast advertising, aims to insure that advertisements are "legal, decent, honest and truthful".

The Labour party, which has been leading the ruling 'Conservative party by about 20 percentage points in polls, is expected to drop its 1992 general election pledge to impose a statutory code of advertising practice. A general election in Britain must be held by spring 1997.

Griffiths said he was starting "with a clean slate" and did not rule out legislation, Campaign reported. Griffiths said Labour aims to make the existing self-regulatory system work better, the paper said.
"There is a problem with repeat offenders," Griffiths told Campaign. "Some people are making a career out of it."

Griffiths said he favours fining advertisers who repeatedly breach the code. Advertisers who continue to transgress after being fined could be banned from advertising the product or even banned from trading altogether, Campaign reported.
